experiment.name: phase2_tier1_validate
_comment: Replication of the tier-1 rate sweep, and a test of what limits it.
The published sweep (results/20260903-115606-phase2_tier1_rate) reports a
241 bit/s capacity peak at a 3 ms symbol on a curve that is not monotone:
the failed repeats excluded makes it monotone and puts the 2 ms row
highest -- 385.6, 241.1, 232.7, 111.9 b/s conditional on acquiring. So the
dips are acquisition failures, not a channel that is worse at 2 ms than at
3, and the published peak is where three coin flips happened to land the
same way. n=3 cannot say otherwise: 3/3 acquired puts the true acquisition
probability in [0.29, 1.00].
Two arms, same rates, same payloads, same session. p13 is the published
13-bit Barker preamble and replicates the sweep. p63 is a 63-bit maximal
length sequence (x^6+x+1, sidelobe 1, balanced 32/63) worth 2.2x in
correlation amplitude -- the only lever left on acquisition, since the
differential correlator was measured and rejected. If acquisition is the
cause, p63 clears the dips and the curve straightens; if the dips survive
a 2.2x longer sync word they are the channel.
Preamble rides in every frame, so p63 costs airtime the capacity column
does not charge it for: 19.7% of each frame against 4.8%. Compare the arms
on capacity to test the acquisition hypothesis, and net of overhead before
quoting a throughput.
1.5 ms is below the floor the ~1 ms RAPL update imposes -- the chip is
0.75 ms, shorter than one sample -- and is here to bracket the peak from
above rather than to work. 8 ms is the anchor: it read 109.6 b/s at 3/3 in
the published sweep, and cross-session comparison has no other check.
The A/A transmits with on == off in each arm, so a longer preamble gets
its own null: more correlation gain is also more chance to lock onto noise.
